title: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review
extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical studies on generative AI (GenAI) use in K-12 education to understand how these tools have been used in teaching and learning, what outcomes have been reported, and what gaps remain. The review responds to a lack of synthesis focused specifically on K-12 practice, as opposed to higher education or general discussions of ChatGPT and related tools.

Using PRISMA and Kitchenham-guided procedures, the author searched Scopus and Web of Science and supplemented the search with snowballing. Thirty empirical papers met the inclusion criteria. The reviewed studies covered mostly high school and middle school settings, with some elementary and broader K-12 work, and the majority were in STEM subjects. ChatGPT was by far the most common tool, often used alone but sometimes alongside Copilot, DALL-E, Bert, Canva, or custom tools based on GPT-4 and DALL·E.

The review finds that quasi-experimental designs were the most common, but many studies relied on self-reported psychological outcomes such as trust, usability, self-efficacy, engagement, and attitudes rather than objective learning measures. The author concludes that GenAI shows promise for supporting learning, problem solving, self-regulation, and teacher development, but the evidence base is still thin in terms of detailed classroom implementation, objective achievement outcomes, teacher-led real-time use, and underrepresented contexts such as early childhood, special education, rural settings, Africa, and non-English scholarship.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review of 30 empirical K-12 GenAI studies, but it is not itself a causal evaluation of a single intervention. The evidence base it summarizes is dominated by quasi-experimental, descriptive, and self-report studies, which limits causal confidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has moderate synthesis value for the field by mapping how GenAI is being used in K-12 and by flagging implementation risks and gaps, but it does not estimate a direct learning effect. Its practical impact is mainly agenda-setting and descriptive rather than demonstrably outcome-changing.
